lines.text: Meat and seafood are primary protein sources in diets around the world. Meat from mammals is categorised as red meat — beef (from cattle), lamb (from sheep), and pork (from pigs) — which is rich in iron and protein. White meat, primarily poultry — chicken, turkey, and duck — is generally leaner. Meat is sold in various cuts: a steak, a chop, a fillet, mince (ground meat), and a joint (a large piece for roasting). At the butcher's, you might ask for a specific cut, thickness, or preparation. Seafood divides into fish and shellfish. Popular fish include salmon, cod, tuna, haddock, and sea bass. Fish can be fresh, frozen, smoked, or tinned. Shellfish includes crustaceans — prawns, lobster, and crab — and molluscs — mussels, oysters, and squid. Seafood is prized for its omega-3 fatty acids and delicate flavour. Cooking methods for meat and seafood are varied: grilling, roasting, frying, poaching, braising, and barbecuing each produce different textures and flavours. Doneness levels for steak — rare, medium-rare, medium, and well-done — are important to know when ordering at a restaurant. Understanding halal and kosher dietary requirements is also essential in multicultural English-speaking environments.

lines.text: English uniquely uses different words for animals and their meat — a legacy of the Norman Conquest (1066). Anglo-Saxon farmers used 'cow, pig, sheep, deer'; French-speaking nobles used 'beef (boeuf), pork (porc), mutton (mouton), venison (venaison)' at the table.

lines.text: When ordering steak, you'll be asked: 'How would you like it cooked?' Respond with: rare (very pink inside), medium-rare (mostly pink), medium (slightly pink), medium-well (barely pink), or well-done (no pink). This vocabulary is essential for dining out.

lines.text: Traditional English shops had specialist food sellers: the 'butcher' (meat), 'fishmonger' (fish), 'greengrocer' (fruit and vegetables), 'baker' (bread). While supermarkets dominate today, these specialist terms are still widely used and tested in exams.
